label: lem:monic
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Existence follows from coercivity on the finite-dimensional affine
space of monic polynomials. Differentiating the norm along $q_n+\varepsilon p$
gives \eqref{eq:orthog}; the zero set of $q_n$ has measure zero, so
dominated convergence justifies the derivative. If $q_n$ had fewer
than $n$ sign changes in $(-1,1)$, the product of its sign-change
factors, with a suitable overall sign, would be a polynomial of degree
less than $n$ whose sign agrees with that of $q_n$. This contradicts
\eqref{eq:orthog}. Hence all $n$ zeros are simple and interior.

For two minimizers, equality in the convexity inequality for the
$L^1$ norm implies agreement of their signs almost everywhere. Their
simple sign-change zeros must therefore coincide, and the monic
normalization makes the polynomials equal. Applying uniqueness to
$(-1)^nq_n(-t)$ proves the last assertion.
head: environment

label: thm:BohrAllDimensions
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $t_1,\ldots,t_n$ for the zeros of $q_{n,d}$. At a point $t\in(-1,1)$ distinct from the nodes, the interpolation remainder is
\[
 G_d(t)-p_{n-1,d}(t)
 =\frac{G_d^{(n)}(\xi)}{n!}\,q_{n,d}(t),
\]
where $\xi$ lies between the smallest and largest of $t,t_1,\ldots,t_n$. By~\eqref{eq:generalGreenDerivatives}, the error therefore has the sign of $q_{n,d}$. Put $s_{n,d}=\operatorname{sgn} q_{n,d}$. For any competing polynomial $p$ of degree less than $n$, the moment conditions give
\[
 \int_{-1}^1|G_d-p|\,d\mu_d
 \geq\int_{-1}^1(G_d-p)s_{n,d}\,d\mu_d
 =\int_{-1}^1G_ds_{n,d}\,d\mu_d,
\]
first for real $p$. For a complex $p$, replacing it by its real part cannot increase its distance from the real kernel. The interpolant attains this lower bound because its error has sign $s_{n,d}$. This proves best approximation and the equality of the two integrals in~\eqref{eq:BohrAllDimensions}.

Now let $f\perp\mathcal H_{<n}$ and put $g=-\Delta f$. The same low harmonics of $g$ vanish. Subtracting the interpolating polynomial from the Green representation at any pole $e$ gives
\[
 f(e)=\int_{S^d}\bigl(G_d(e\cdot\omega)-p_{n-1,d}(e\cdot\omega)\bigr)
 g(\omega)\,d\sigma_d(\omega).
\]
The first integral in~\eqref{eq:BohrAllDimensions} is therefore an upper bound for the Bohr constant.

For the reverse bound, take $g_0(\omega)=s_{n,d}(e\cdot\omega)$. This function is bounded by one and is orthogonal to $\mathcal H_{<n}$. To see the orthogonality, average a spherical harmonic of degree less than $n$ over the rotations fixing $e$. The average is a polynomial of that degree in $e\cdot\omega$, and~\eqref{eq:generalSignMoments} applies. The mean-zero Green potential of $g_0$ is the function $f_{n,d}$ in~\eqref{eq:generalBohrExtremal}; convolution preserves the missing harmonics. This potential is continuous, since rotations of an integrable zonal kernel are continuous in its integral norm. At $e$ it takes exactly the value of the second integral in~\eqref{eq:BohrAllDimensions}. The same kernel bound applies at every pole to this bounded source, proving~\eqref{eq:generalBohrExtremalValue}.

Finally, apply the spherical heat semigroup to $g_0$. It preserves the missing harmonics and the bound by one, and produces smooth functions $g_\varepsilon$. Their mean-zero Green potentials $f_\varepsilon$ are smooth, have the same missing harmonics, and satisfy $-\Delta f_\varepsilon=g_\varepsilon$. The smoothed sign functions converge to $g_0$ away from its finitely many latitude spheres of discontinuity. Since $G_d\in L^1(\mu_d)$, dominated convergence gives
\[
 f_\varepsilon(e)\longrightarrow
 \int_{-1}^1G_d(t)s_{n,d}(t)\,d\mu_d(t).
\]
This proves the matching lower bound within the smooth class used to define $H(n,S^d)$.
head: environment

label: prop:evenGreenStructure
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Away from the pole, the mean-zero Green kernel satisfies
\[
 (1-t^2)G_{2s}''(t)-2stG_{2s}'(t)=1.
\]
Substituting the right-hand side of~\eqref{eq:evenGreenStructure} into this equation gives~\eqref{eq:evenGreenRecurrence}. More explicitly, the zonal Laplacian sends $(1-t)^{-j}$ to
\[
 2j(j+1-s)(1-t)^{-j-1}+j(2s-j-1)(1-t)^{-j},
\]
and sends $-\log((1-t)/2)$ to $(2s-1)-(2s-2)/(1-t)$. Cancellation of the first pole gives $b_1$, and cancellation of each subsequent pole gives the recurrence. The highest possible pole cancels because its coefficient contains $j+1-s$ with $j=s-1$. When $s=1$ the logarithm alone satisfies the equation.

The resulting function is regular at $t=-1$ and integrable against $\mu_{2s}$. Writing the differential equation in divergence form gives
\[
 \frac{d}{dt}\left[c_{2s}(1-t^2)^sG_{2s}'(t)\right]
 =c_{2s}(1-t^2)^{s-1}.
\]
The flux vanishes at $t=-1$ and tends to one at $t=1$, since the measure on the right has total mass one. Thus the distributional equation is $-\Delta_{S^{2s}}G_{2s}=\delta_e-1$. Fixing the mean identifies the function with the Green kernel in~\eqref{eq:generalGreenPoisson}. Positivity of the coefficients follows directly from the recurrence.
head: environment

label: thm:trigGreenApproximation
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The sine interpolant exists and is unique by discrete sine orthogonality on the grid~\eqref{eq:uniformGreenNodes}. Oddness extends the interpolation to the equally spaced grid on the full circle; the values at $0$ and $\pi$ are automatically zero. We first show why the error changes sign precisely at these nodes. The useful observation is that the coefficients in~\eqref{eq:trigGreenFourier} are positive integrals of geometric sequences.

For $0<\rho<1$, put
\[
 F_\rho(\theta)=\frac{\sin\theta}{1-2\rho\cos\theta+\rho^2}
 =\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\rho^{k-1}\sin(k\theta),
\]
and denote sine interpolation on our grid by $\mathcal I_n$. Write $N=n+1$. On this grid, the frequencies $2mN+k$ and $2mN-k$ give, respectively, $\sin(k\theta_j)$ and $-\sin(k\theta_j)$, while multiples of $N$ vanish. Summing the resulting geometric sequences gives
\[
 \mathcal I_nF_\rho(\theta)
 =\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{\rho^{k-1}-\rho^{2N-k-1}}{1-\rho^{2N}}\sin(k\theta).
\]
Subtracting this finite sum from $F_\rho$ yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:geometricSineRemainder}
 F_\rho(\theta)-\mathcal I_nF_\rho(\theta)
 =\frac{\rho^n(1-\rho^2)\sin(N\theta)}
 {(1-\rho^{2N})(1-2\rho\cos\theta+\rho^2)}.
\end{equation}
Every factor apart from $\sin(N\theta)$ is positive.

For $k\geq2$, we have $2/(k^2-1)=\int_0^1(1-\rho^2)\rho^{k-2}\,d\rho$. Consequently~\eqref{eq:trigGreenFourier} can be written as
\[
 \mathcal G_2(\theta)=\left(2\log2-\frac32\right)\sin\theta
 +\int_0^1\frac{1-\rho^2}{\rho}\bigl(F_\rho(\theta)-\sin\theta\bigr)\,d\rho.
\]
The summable Fourier coefficients justify integration term by term. Interpolation commutes with this integral because it is a finite linear combination of the values at the nodes. Since it reproduces $\sin\theta$, formula~\eqref{eq:geometricSineRemainder} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:positiveTrigRemainder}
 \mathcal G_2(\theta)-t_n(\theta)
 =\sin((n+1)\theta)\int_0^1
 \frac{\rho^{n-1}(1-\rho^2)^2\,d\rho}
 {(1-\rho^{2n+2})(1-2\rho\cos\theta+\rho^2)}.
\end{equation}
For $0<\theta<\pi$, the integral is finite and strictly positive. This proves the asserted sign of the error; oddness gives the same sign identity on the negative half-period.

The reason this sign pattern proves best approximation is that the function $s(\theta)=\operatorname{sgn}\sin((n+1)\theta)$ annihilates $T_n$. Indeed, its Fourier series is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:S2squarewave}
 s(\theta)=\frac4\pi\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}
 \frac{\sin((2j+1)(n+1)\theta)}{2j+1},
\end{equation}
and all its frequencies exceed $n$. Therefore, for every $t\in T_n$,
\[
 \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|\mathcal G_2-t|\,d\theta
 \geq\left|\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}(\mathcal G_2-t)s\,d\theta\right|
 =\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|\mathcal G_2-t_n|\,d\theta.
\]
This proves minimality. Finally, insert~\eqref{eq:trigGreenFourier} and~\eqref{eq:S2squarewave} into $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\mathcal G_2s\,d\theta$. Orthogonality of the sine functions gives~\eqref{eq:trigGreenBestError}; the calculation is justified by $L^2$ convergence.
head: environment

label: thm:sphere2
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $g=-\Delta f$ and fix a pole $e\in S^2$. If $f\perp\mathcal H_{<n}$ and $\left\|g\right\|_\infty\leq1$, estimate~\eqref{eq:kernelApproximationBound} applies with $t_{n-1}=0$. Taking the interpolating polynomial $p_{n-1}$ from Section~\ref{sec:zonalapproximation} and using~\eqref{eq:zonalBestApproximation} gives the asserted upper bound. The matching lower bound comes from the sign of the kernel's interpolation error.

To prove sharpness in the smooth class, start with the bounded zonal function $g_0(\omega)=s_n(e\cdot\omega)$. Formula~\eqref{eq:S2zonal} and~\eqref{eq:S2annihilator} show that $g_0\perp\mathcal H_{<n}$. We approximate it by smooth functions without increasing its norm or introducing low harmonics. For a positive integer $m$, set
\[
 a_m(t)=(m+1)\left(\frac{1+t}{2}\right)^m,
 \qquad
 g_m(\omega)=\int_{S^2}a_m(\omega\cdot\eta)g_0(\eta)\,d\sigma_2(\eta).
\]
The kernel is nonnegative and $\frac12\int_{-1}^1a_m(t)\,dt=1$, so $\left\|g_m\right\|_\infty\leq1$. Each $g_m$ is a spherical polynomial. Formula~\eqref{eq:S2zonal} shows that this convolution acts by a scalar on every harmonic subspace, hence $g_m\perp\mathcal H_{<n}$. Finally, for $0<\delta<2$, its mass on $t\leq1-\delta$ is $(1-\delta/2)^{m+1}$. Consequently $g_m$ tends to $g_0$ at every continuity point of $g_0$, and therefore almost everywhere.

Let $f_m$ be the mean-zero Green potential of $g_m$. It is a smooth spherical polynomial, satisfies $-\Delta f_m=g_m$, and has no harmonics of degrees below $n$. Dominated convergence in~\eqref{eq:GreenRepresentation} now gives
\[
 f_m(e)\longrightarrow\int_{S^2}G_2(e\cdot\omega)g_0(\omega)\,d\sigma_2(\omega)
 =\frac12\int_{-1}^1G_2(t)s_n(t)\,dt.
\]
Every $f_m$ is admissible in~\eqref{eq:sphericalBohrFavard}. The lower bound obtained from $\left\|f_m\right\|_\infty\geq|f_m(e)|$ matches~\eqref{eq:S2besterror}. We have proved
\begin{equation}\label{eq:H22integral}
 H(n,S^2)=\frac12\int_0^\pi G_2(\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,\operatorname{sgn}\sin((n+1)\theta)\,d\theta.
\end{equation}

The value of this integral was computed in Section~\ref{sec:zonalapproximation}. Combining~\eqref{eq:S2besterror} with~\eqref{eq:zonalBestApproximation} proves~\eqref{eq:H22fixed}.

For each positive odd integer $k$,
\[
 0\leq\frac{n^2}{k\bigl((n+1)^2k^2-1\bigr)}\leq\frac1{k^3},
 \qquad
 \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n^2}{k\bigl((n+1)^2k^2-1\bigr)}=\frac1{k^3}.
\]
Dominated convergence in~\eqref{eq:H22fixed} gives
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}n^2H(n,S^2)=2\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac1{(2j+1)^3}=\frac74\zeta(3).
\]
The same termwise bound shows that $n^2H(n,S^2)\leq7\zeta(3)/4$ for every $n$. Since the exact fixed-$n$ bounds were obtained within the smooth class, their limit proves both~\eqref{eq:H22} and the sharpness of~\eqref{eq:S2Bohr}.
head: environment

label: thm:S3fixedn
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: eq:Stieltjes
title: Proof
body_md:
The following representation makes the sign of the Green interpolation
error visible:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Stieltjes}
 G_3(t)=-\frac14+\int_1^\infty\frac{a}{2\sqrt{a^2-1}}
 \left(\frac1{a-t}-\frac1a\right)\,da.
\end{equation}
Indeed, putting $a=\cosh u$ reduces the integral to
$\tfrac t2\int_0^\infty(\cosh u-t)^{-1}\,du$. For $t=\cos\theta$
this equals $\tfrac12(\pi-\theta)\cot\theta$.

Let $p_{n-1}$ interpolate $G_3$ at the zeros of $q_n$. Interpolation
of $(a-t)^{-1}$ has the exact remainder
$q_n(t)/((a-t)q_n(a))$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:remainder3}
 G_3(t)-p_{n-1}(t)
 =q_n(t)\int_1^\infty
 \frac{a\,da}{2\sqrt{a^2-1}(a-t)q_n(a)}.
\end{equation}
The integral is strictly positive for $-1<t<1$, since $q_n$ has all its zeros in that interval and is monic. Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:error-sign}
 \operatorname{sgn}(G_3-p_{n-1})=\operatorname{sgn} q_n.
\end{equation}
Integrating the error of any competing polynomial against $\operatorname{sgn} q_n$ and using~\eqref{eq:q3orthog} gives a lower bound for its $L^1(\mu_3)$ norm. By~\eqref{eq:error-sign}, the interpolant attains that bound. This proves minimality and the second equality in~\eqref{eq:sharp-sign}; estimate~\eqref{eq:upperapprox} gives the corresponding upper bound for $H(n,S^3)$.

It remains to prove sharpness within the smooth class of~\eqref{eq:sphericalBohrFavard}. The zonal function $g(\omega)=\operatorname{sgn} q_n(e\cdot\omega)$
annihilates $\mathcal H_{<n}$: average a spherical harmonic over
rotations fixing $e$ and use \eqref{eq:orthog}. Its Green potential
attains the value on the right of \eqref{eq:sharp-sign} at $e$.
Apply the spherical heat semigroup to $g$. This preserves the gap and
does not increase its supremum norm. The corresponding smooth Green
potentials converge at $e$, since $G_3$ is integrable and the smoothed
sign functions converge almost everywhere. Together with
\eqref{eq:upperapprox}, this proves \eqref{eq:sharp-sign}.
head: environment

label: prop:S3reciprocal
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $P_m(t)=A_m(\cos t)$, and denote its zeros on $(0,\pi)$ by $t_1<\cdots<t_m$. Put $x_j=\cos t_j$ and $\varepsilon_j=(-1)^{j-1}$. Applying~\eqref{eq:S3cosineReproduction} to $\cos kt$ and integrating by parts gives
\[
 2\sum_{j=1}^m\varepsilon_j\sin(kt_j)=k\ell_m,
 \qquad k=1,\ldots,m.
\]
Since $\sin kt=\sin t\,U_{k-1}(\cos t)$ and $U_{k-1}(1)=k$, these identities reproduce evaluation at $1$ for every algebraic polynomial of degree less than $m$. Applying them to the Lagrange basis at $x_1,\ldots,x_m$, and using $A_m(1)=1$, yields
\[
 \frac1{A_m'(x_j)}
 =\frac{2\varepsilon_j(1-x_j)\sin t_j}{\ell_m}.
\]
Now expand $1/A_m(v)$ in simple fractions and use
\[
 \int_0^\infty\frac{d\eta}{\cosh\eta-\cos t}
 =\frac{\pi-t}{\sin t},\qquad 0<t<\pi.
\]
It follows that the right-hand side of~\eqref{eq:S3finiteReciprocal} is
\[
 \frac1{2\pi}\sum_{j=1}^m
 \varepsilon_j(\pi-t_j)(1-\cos t_j).
\]
To identify this sum with the Bohr constant, pair $\theta$ and $\pi-\theta$ in~\eqref{eq:sharp-sign}, and then put $t=2\theta$. The term involving $1-\cos t$ vanishes by~\eqref{eq:S3cosineReproduction}, leaving
\[
 H(2m,S^3)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_0^\pi
 (\pi-t)\sin t\,s_m(t)\,dt.
\]
Integration by parts over the sign intervals gives the preceding sum: the remaining terms cancel because~\eqref{eq:S3cosineReproduction} gives $\int s_m=\int s_m\cos t=\ell_m$. This proves the formula.
head: environment

label: lem:point
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:point}
The function $Q_n$ minimizes
\[
 J(T)=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}|T(\theta)|\,d\theta
\]
over $T\in\mathcal T_n'$ with $T(0)=1$. Furthermore,
$\left\|Q_n\right\|_\infty=1$ on $\mathbb R$ and $|F_n(z)|\leq e^{|\operatorname{Im}z|}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First take real even $T$. It is a polynomial in $t=\cos\theta$ of
parity $n$. A variation vanishing at $\theta=0$ also vanishes at
$t=-1$, and hence has the form $(1-t^2)p(t)$ with $\deg p\leq n-2$.
After the change of variable $t=\cos\theta$, the first variation of
$J$ at $Q_n$ is zero by \eqref{eq:q3orthog}. Convexity gives
minimality. Taking the real part and then averaging under
$\theta\mapsto-\theta$ reduces an arbitrary complex competitor to
this case without increasing its norm or changing its value at zero.

The modulus of every member of $\mathcal T_n'$ is $\pi$-periodic.
If $|Q_n(\theta_0)|>1$, translating by $\theta_0$ and dividing by
$Q_n(\theta_0)$ produces a competitor with smaller $J$. Thus
$\left\|Q_n\right\|_\infty=1$. The Bernstein bound for trigonometric
polynomials gives $|Q_n(z)|\leq e^{n|\operatorname{Im}z|}$ and
proves the assertion about $F_n$.
head: environment

label: thm:S3asymptotic
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: prop:convergence
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first construct competitors. Let $F$ be a real even Schwartz
function of exponential type strictly less than one, with $F(0)=1$.
Its periodization
\[
 T_n(\theta)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}(-1)^{nj}
 F\bigl(n(\theta+j\pi)\bigr)
\]
belongs to $\mathcal T_n'$. Indeed, Poisson summation restricts its
frequencies to integers of parity $n$, and the support of $\widehat F$
restricts their absolute values to less than $n$. Also,
\[
 T_n(0)\longrightarrow1,\qquad
 J(T_n)\leq\frac1n\left\|F\right\|_1.
\]
Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:point} to $T_n/T_n(0)$ for all sufficiently large $n$ gives $\limsup m_n\leq\left\|F\right\|_1$.

Such competitors can approximate $\varphi$ in $L^1$. For example, choose a real even Schwartz function $\psi$ of type at most one with $\psi(0)=1$ and $|\psi|\leq1$, and use $\varphi((1-2\varepsilon)x)\psi(\varepsilon x)$ for $0<\varepsilon<1/2$. Dilation continuity in $L^1$, followed by dominated convergence for the multiplier, proves convergence to $\varphi$. Hence $\limsup m_n\leq M$.

The bound in Lemma~\ref{lem:point} makes $(F_n)$ a normal family. Choose a subsequence along which $m_n$ tends to its lower limit, and then a locally uniformly convergent further subsequence. Its limit $F_*$ has type at most one and $F_*(0)=1$. Fatou's lemma on expanding real intervals gives $\left\|F_*\right\|_1\leq\liminf m_n$, whereas~\eqref{eq:HB} gives $M\leq\left\|F_*\right\|_1$. Together with the upper bound already proved, this shows that $m_n\to M$. For any locally uniform subsequential limit the same argument now gives norm $M$, so uniqueness forces that limit to be $\varphi$. This proves convergence of the full sequence. Subtracting the integral on $[-R,R]$ from~\eqref{eq:mass}, and then letting $R$ grow, proves~\eqref{eq:tight}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It is enough first to consider $n=2m$. The definitions give $P_m(t)=Q_{2m}(t/2)$, $\ell_m=J(Q_{2m})$, and $F_{2m}(z)=P_m(z/m)$. Rescaling~\eqref{eq:S3finiteReciprocal} therefore gives
\[
 (2m)^2H(2m,S^3)=\frac{m_{2m}}{2\pi}
 \int_0^\infty\frac{dy}{F_{2m}(iy)}.
\]
Proposition~\ref{prop:convergence} gives $m_{2m}\to M$ and local convergence of the denominator to $\varphi(iy)$. To pass to the limit in the integral, note that the opposite pairs of roots of $q_{2m}$ give
\[
 F_{2m}(iy)=\prod_{j=1}^m
 \left(1+\frac{\sinh^2(y/(2m))}{1-r_j^2}\right),
\]
where $r_j$ are its positive roots. All coefficients in the power series in $y^2$ are nonnegative. Since $-F_{2m}''(0)/2\to c_0>0$, there is a fixed $c>0$ such that $F_{2m}(iy)\geq1+cy^2$ for all sufficiently large $m$ and all $y\geq0$. Dominated convergence proves the limit along the even degrees.

Finally, $H(n,S^3)$ is nonincreasing in $n$, by its best-kernel-approximation characterization. Thus $H(2m+2,S^3)\leq H(2m+1,S^3)\leq H(2m,S^3)$, and multiplying by $(2m+1)^2$ gives the same limit along the odd degrees.
head: environment

label: thm:main
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: lem:B
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For fixed $y$, the poles at $z=\pm iy$ in \eqref{eq:B} are removable
because $\varphi$ is even. This remains locally uniform at $z=y=0$:
write $\varphi(z)=H(z^2)$ and use the divided difference of $H$.
For large $y$, the integrand is locally bounded by a constant times
$y^{-2}$. Thus the integral defines an entire even function.

Here is also a growth bound, to make the spectral support explicit.
For $|z|=R\geq2$, split the integral at $2R$. The tail is bounded
by $C e^{|\operatorname{Im}z|}/R$. In $0\leq y\leq2R$, away from
unit neighborhoods of $z=iy$ and $z=-iy$, the two denominator
factors have modulus at least one, giving a bound
$CR e^{|\operatorname{Im}z|}$. In either neighborhood cancel the
nearby factor by the divided-difference formula. Cauchy's estimate
and $|\varphi(z)|\leq e^{|\operatorname{Im}z|}$ bound the resulting
derivative by $Ce^{|\operatorname{Im}z|}$, while the other factor
has modulus comparable to $R$. These bounds prove
\[
 |B(z)|\leq C(1+|z|)e^{|\operatorname{Im}z|}.
\]
The constants here are independent of $z$.

Since $(2/\pi)\int_0^\infty(x^2+y^2)^{-1}\,dy=1/x$,
formula \eqref{eq:Berror} follows. Polar coordinates and~\eqref{eq:betaDouble} then give
\[
 \left\|\mathcal K\right\|_1=\int_0^\infty x^2\left|x^{-1}-B(x)\right|\,dx
 =\beta.
\]
The one-dimensional Paley--Wiener theorem for distributions implies
$\operatorname{supp}\widehat B\subset[-1,1]$. The radial Fourier identity
\[
 \widehat{B(|\cdot|)}_{\mathbb R^3}(\rho)
 =-\frac{2\pi}{\rho}\frac d{d\rho}\widehat B_{\mathbb R}(\rho),
 \qquad\rho>0,
\]
follows by differentiating the one-dimensional cosine transform in the radial Fourier formula, and remains valid for tempered distributions. It shows that the radial lift has spectrum in the unit ball. The Fourier transform of
$(4\pi|u|)^{-1}$ is $|\xi|^{-2}$. This proves the multiplier
identity outside that ball. Since $\mathcal K\in L^1$, its Fourier transform
is continuous; the same identity holds on the boundary.
head: environment

label: eq:zonalexp
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $f\perp\mathcal H_{<n}$. Fix a pole $e$ and average $f$ over rotations fixing $e$. This
preserves $f(e)$, preserves the gap, and does not increase
$\left\|\Delta f\right\|_\infty$. Thus we may assume that $f$ and
$g=-\Delta f$ are zonal. Write $g(x)=\gamma(e\cdot x)$. The zonal harmonics on $S^3$ are
$U_\ell(\cos\theta)=\sin((\ell+1)\theta)/\sin\theta$. We may write
\begin{equation}\label{eq:zonalexp}
 \gamma(\cos\theta)\sin\theta=\sum_{k\geq n+1}b_k\sin k\theta,
 \qquad
 f(e)=\sum_{k\geq n+1}\frac{k b_k}{k^2-1}.
\end{equation}
For smooth $g$ the coefficients decrease rapidly. Multiplication by $\cos r$ will replace each frequency $k$ by $k-1$ and $k+1$. Dividing by $r$ then gives the radial Euclidean waves on which the inverse multiplier is known. This motivates the bounded function on $\mathbb R^3$
\begin{equation}\label{eq:h}
 h(u)=\frac{\sin r\cos r}{r}\gamma(\cos r),\qquad r=|u|,
\end{equation}
with the continuous value at zero. Then
$\left\|h\right\|_\infty\leq\left\|g\right\|_\infty$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hshells}
 h(u)=\frac12\sum_{k\geq n+1}b_k
 \left(\frac{\sin((k+1)r)}r+\frac{\sin((k-1)r)}r\right).
\end{equation}
All frequencies here are at least $n$.

Scale the kernel by $\mathcal K_n(u)=n\mathcal K(nu)$. Then
$\left\|\mathcal K_n\right\|_1=\beta/n^2$ and
$\widehat{\mathcal K_n}(\xi)=|\xi|^{-2}$ for $|\xi|\geq n$.
The spherical average of a plane wave is
\[
 \int_{S^2}e^{i\lambda\omega\cdot u}\,d\sigma_2(\omega)
 =\frac{\sin(\lambda r)}{\lambda r}.
\]
Consequently, for $\lambda\geq n$,
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R^3}\mathcal K_n(u)\frac{\sin(\lambda|u|)}{|u|}\,du
 =\lambda\widehat{\mathcal K_n}(\lambda)=\frac1\lambda.
\]
Integrating \eqref{eq:hshells} term by term is justified by rapid
decay of the coefficients and $\mathcal K_n\in L^1$. Using
\eqref{eq:zonalexp}, we obtain
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R^3}\mathcal K_n(u)h(u)\,du
 =\frac12\sum_{k\geq n+1}b_k
 \left(\frac1{k+1}+\frac1{k-1}\right)=f(e).
\]
It follows that
\[
 |f(e)|\leq\frac\beta{n^2}\left\|g\right\|_\infty.
\]
The pole was arbitrary, so this proves~\eqref{eq:H23}. The limit in Theorem~\ref{thm:S3asymptotic} shows that the coefficient cannot be decreased, and hence $H(S^3)=\beta$.
head: environment

label: lem:generalEndpointMinimum
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Taking real parts and then averaging under $\theta\mapsto-\theta$ reduces the minimization to $T(\theta)=P(\cos\theta)$, where $P$ is a real polynomial of degree at most $n$ and parity $n$. The difference of two admissible polynomials vanishes at both $1$ and $-1$, so it has the form $(1-t^2)p(t)$ with $\deg p\leq n-2$. On changing variables in~\eqref{eq:generalEndpointNorm}, the measure becomes $(1-t^2)^{(d-4)/2}\,dt$. The additional factor $1-t^2$ in a variation restores the weight in~\eqref{eq:generalSignMoments}. Those moments therefore make the first variation vanish at $Q_{n,d}$, and convexity of the absolute value proves minimality. This also explains the exponent $d-3$ in the angular weight.

To prove the uniform bound when the weight is nonconstant, regard $q_{n,d}(e\cdot\omega)/q_{n,d}(1)$ as a zonal polynomial on $S^{d-2}$. The angular surface measure on this sphere is proportional to $\sin^{d-3}\theta\,d\theta$. Consider all spherical polynomials of degree at most $n$ and parity $n$. Averaging over the orthogonal transformations fixing $e$ preserves the value at $e$ and does not increase the integral norm; the average is a zonal polynomial of the form already considered. Thus our polynomial minimizes the integral norm in this larger space as well, subject to its value at $e$ being one. If its modulus exceeded one at another point, moving that point to $e$ by an orthogonal transformation and dividing by the resulting value at $e$ would decrease the norm. This contradiction proves the uniform bound. For $S^1$ the averaging includes reflection across the axis through $e$. Finally, the Bernstein bound for trigonometric polynomials, followed by the scaling in~\eqref{eq:generalEndpointScaling}, gives the stated bound on $\mathbb C$.
head: environment

label: prop:weightedEndpointConvergence
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\alpha=d-3$. The proof follows the periodization argument used for $S^3$, but we keep the weight in order to control the tails. Let $F$ be real and even, of exponential type strictly less than one, and Schwartz on the real line, with $F(0)=1$. Its periodization
\[
 T_n(\theta)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}(-1)^{nj}F\bigl(n(\theta+j\pi)\bigr)
\]
belongs to $\mathcal T_n'$ by Poisson summation, and $T_n(0)\to1$. The triangle inequality and $n|\sin(x/n)|\leq|x|$ give
\[
 n^{\alpha+1}J_d(T_n)\leq\int_\mathbb R|F(x)|\,|x|^\alpha\,dx.
\]
Such functions approximate $\Phi_d$ in the weighted integral norm. Indeed, choose a real even Schwartz function $\psi$ of type at most one with $\psi(0)=1$ and $|\psi|\leq1$, and use $\Phi_d((1-2\varepsilon)x)\psi(\varepsilon x)$. These functions have type less than one; dilation continuity and dominated convergence prove the approximation as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. The extremal function belongs also to ordinary $L^1(\mathbb R)$, and its derivatives are bounded on the real line, so the products are Schwartz. Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:generalEndpointMinimum} to $T_n/T_n(0)$ proves the upper bound
\[
 \limsup_{n\to\infty}n^{\alpha+1}J_d(Q_{n,d})\leq M_d.
\]

The same lemma makes the functions $F_{n,d}$ a normal family. With $w_n(x)=n|\sin(x/n)|$, the norm being considered is
\[
 m_{n,d}:=n^{\alpha+1}J_d(Q_{n,d})
 =\int_{-\pi n/2}^{\pi n/2}|F_{n,d}(x)|\,w_n(x)^\alpha\,dx.
\]
Choose a subsequence realizing the lower limit of $m_{n,d}$ and then a locally uniformly convergent further subsequence. Its limit $F_*$ is real and even, has type at most one, and satisfies $F_*(0)=1$. Since $w_n(x)\to|x|$ locally, Fatou's lemma on bounded intervals, followed by expansion of the intervals, gives
\[
 M_d\leq\int_\mathbb R|F_*(x)|\,|x|^\alpha\,dx
 \leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}m_{n,d}.
\]
Together with the upper bound this proves convergence of the minimum values. Every locally uniform subsequential limit must now be a minimizer in~\eqref{eq:weightedEntireMinimum}; uniqueness gives convergence of the full sequence to $\Phi_d$.

Subtracting the integral over $[-R,R]$ from $m_{n,d}$ proves tightness of the mass with weight $w_n^\alpha$. On the expanding interval, $w_n(x)\geq2|x|/\pi$. For $b<\alpha$ and $|x|>R$, the ratio $w_n(x)^b/w_n(x)^\alpha$ is therefore at most $(\pi/(2R))^{\alpha-b}$. This bounds the tails for every lower weight in the proposition; local convergence supplies the integrals on $[-R,R]$. The case $b=\alpha$ follows from the already established mass convergence, proving~\eqref{eq:weightedMomentConvergence}.
head: environment

label: lem:generalOutsideIntegral
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
All zeros of $F_{n,d}$ are real, since the zeros of $q_{n,d}$ lie in $(-1,1)$. Hurwitz's theorem and Proposition~\ref{prop:weightedEndpointConvergence} imply that all zeros of $\Phi_d$ are real as well. There are infinitely many: otherwise Hadamard factorization and evenness would make $\Phi_d$ a polynomial, contrary to its weighted integrability. Also $\Phi_d(0)=1$. Choose two positive zeros, counted with multiplicity. Local convergence supplies two corresponding roots $r_1,r_2$ of $q_{n,d}$ near one, for which $n\arccos r_j$ stays bounded.

Put $A(a)=q_{n,d}(a)/q_{n,d}(1)$ and let $\epsilon$ be the parity of $n$. Factoring over the positive roots $r_j$ gives
\[
 A(a)=a^\epsilon\prod_{j=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}
 \left(1+\frac{a^2-1}{1-r_j^2}\right).
\]
For $a=\sqrt{1+s^2/n^2}$, the two roots just selected show that $A(a)\geq(1+cs^2)^2$, with a fixed $c>0$, for all $s\geq0$ and all sufficiently large $n$. Since $a\,da=s\,ds/n^2$, the integral in~\eqref{eq:generalOutsideIntegral} is at most
\[
 \frac1{n^2}\int_0^\infty\frac{s\,ds}{(1+cs^2)^2}.
\]
This proves the estimate.
head: environment

label: thm:BohrLimitsFourSix
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We separate the pole terms from the logarithm. Each nonconstant term of the kernels~\eqref{eq:S4Green} and~\eqref{eq:S6Green} has positive derivatives of every positive order. Its interpolation remainder therefore has the sign of $q_{n,d}$. Since the coefficients are positive, the integral errors of the terms add exactly.

For either dimension write $A(t)=q_{n,d}(t)/q_{n,d}(1)$, and let $I$ denote interpolation at the zeros of $q_{n,d}$. For $a>1$, polynomial division gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:generalResolventRemainder}
 \frac1{a-t}-I\left[\frac1{a-t}\right]
 =\frac{A(t)}{(a-t)A(a)}.
\end{equation}
Integrating this identity in $a$ gives the remainder for $-\log((1-t)/2)$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:generalLogRemainder}
 A(t)\int_1^\infty\frac{da}{(a-t)A(a)}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, the logarithm is the integral of $(a-t)^{-1}-(a+1)^{-1}$ from one to infinity, and the second term is constant in $t$ and is reproduced by $I$.

For $d=4$, setting $a=1$ in~\eqref{eq:generalResolventRemainder} shows that the pole contributes
\[
 \frac14\int_{-1}^1|A(t)|(1+t)\,dt
 =\frac14\int_{-1}^1|A(t)|\,dt
 =\frac14J_4(Q_{n,4}).
\]
Here $|A|$ is even. By Proposition~\ref{prop:weightedEndpointConvergence}, this contribution, multiplied by $n^2$, tends to $M_4/4$.

To estimate the logarithmic contribution $L_{n,4}$, pair $t$ and $-t$ in~\eqref{eq:generalLogRemainder}. Since $A(a)>0$ for $a\geq1$, this gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 L_{n,4}
 &=\frac12\int_0^1|A(t)|(1-t^2)
       \int_1^\infty\frac{a\,da}{(a^2-t^2)A(a)}\,dt\\
 &\leq\frac12\left(\int_0^1|A(t)|\,dt\right)
       \left(\int_1^\infty\frac{a\,da}{A(a)}\right).
 \end{aligned}
\]
We used $(1-t^2)/(a^2-t^2)\leq1$. The first factor is $O(n^{-2})$ by~\eqref{eq:weightedMomentConvergence}, and the second is $O(n^{-2})$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:generalOutsideIntegral}. Thus $L_{n,4}=O(n^{-4})$, proving the first limit.

For $d=6$, put $\lambda_n=A'(1)$ and abbreviate
\[
 J_{0,n}=\int_{-1}^1|A(t)|\,dt,
 \qquad J_{1,n}=\int_{-1}^1|A(t)|(1-t^2)\,dt.
\]
These integrals correspond to the angular weights $|\sin\theta|$ and $|\sin\theta|^3$. Differentiating~\eqref{eq:generalResolventRemainder} with respect to $a$, changing the sign, and setting $a=1$ yields
\[
 \frac1{(1-t)^2}-I\left[\frac1{(1-t)^2}\right]
 =A(t)\left(\frac1{(1-t)^2}+\frac{\lambda_n}{1-t}\right).
\]
Multiply by the weight in~\eqref{eq:S6Green} and pair opposite points. The double pole contributes $[2J_{0,n}+(\lambda_n-1)J_{1,n}]/16$, and the simple pole contributes $3J_{1,n}/16$. Their sum is therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:S6PoleContribution}
 \frac{2J_{0,n}+(\lambda_n+2)J_{1,n}}{16}.
\end{equation}
Proposition~\ref{prop:weightedEndpointConvergence}, together with local convergence of derivatives, gives
\[
 n^2J_{0,n}\longrightarrow\int_\mathbb R|\Phi_6(x)|\,|x|\,dx,
 \qquad n^4J_{1,n}\longrightarrow M_6,
 \qquad \frac{\lambda_n}{n^2}=-F_{n,6}''(0)\longrightarrow-\Phi_6''(0).
\]
These are precisely the terms in the second limit of~\eqref{eq:BohrLimitsFourSix}.

Finally, the logarithmic contribution on $S^6$ satisfies
\[
 0\leq L_{n,6}\leq\frac38
 \left(\int_0^1|A(t)|(1-t^2)\,dt\right)
 \left(\int_1^\infty\frac{a\,da}{A(a)}\right).
\]
The estimate follows by the same pairing as above, now with the weight $(1-t^2)^2$. Its factors are $O(n^{-4})$ and $O(n^{-2})$, so $L_{n,6}=O(n^{-6})$. It does not contribute to the limit, completing the proof.
head: environment

label: thm:evenBohrUniform
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: lem:gapTransfer
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First we check the moments before dilation. Under the substitution $t=(s-b)/(1-bs)$, formula~\eqref{eq:mobiusSource} gives
\[
 h_b(t)\,d\mu_d(t)
 =C_b(1-bs)^{n-1}s_n(s)\,d\mu_d(s),\qquad
 C_b=\frac{(1+b)^{d/2}}{(1-b)^{n+d/2-1}}.
\]
For a polynomial $p$ of degree less than $n$, the expression $(1-bs)^{n-1}p((s-b)/(1-bs))$ is again a polynomial of degree less than $n$. Thus~\eqref{eq:generalSignMoments} shows that $h_b$ has gap $n$. Equivalently, the even periodic function $W(\theta)=h_b(\cos\theta)|\sin\theta|^{d-1}$ has no cosine frequencies below $n$. Multiplication of~\eqref{eq:dilatedSource} by $\sin^{d-1}\theta$ gives $m^{-(d-1)}W(m\theta)$, whose frequencies are at least $mn$. Since every polynomial of degree less than $mn$ in $\cos\theta$ is a cosine polynomial of that degree, this proves the spherical gap.

The function $h_b$ itself need not be bounded by one; its increase is compensated by the dilation factor. Put $x=\arccos(\cos(m\theta))$. Because $m$ is even, $x/m\leq\theta\leq\pi-x/m$, and hence $\sin\theta\geq\sin(x/m)$. The finite cosine identity gives
\[
 \frac{\sin x}{m\sin(x/m)}
 =\frac1m\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\cos\left(\left(1-\frac{2j+1}{m}\right)x\right)
 \leq1-\frac c3(1-\cos x).
\]
Indeed, concavity of sine on $[0,\pi/2]$ implies $\cos(ax)\leq1-a^2(1-\cos x)$ when $|a|\leq1$ and $0\leq x\leq\pi$, and the average of the squared coefficients in this sum is $c/3$. Write $N=n+d-1$ and $u=1-\cos x$. Bernoulli's inequality, with exponent $N/(d-1)\geq1$, now yields
\[
 \left(1-\frac{cu}{3}\right)^{d-1}
 \leq\left(1-\frac{(d-1)cu}{3N}\right)^N
 =\left(\frac{1+b\cos x}{1+b}\right)^N.
\]
This is precisely the reciprocal of the amplitude in~\eqref{eq:mobiusSource}. The product in~\eqref{eq:dilatedSource} is therefore bounded by one. Endpoint values, which do not affect the source as an $L^\infty$ function, may be assigned arbitrarily.
head: environment

label: eq:S4PoleLogComparison
title: Proof
body_md:
We first treat $S^4$. Put $R_n=E_1/3$ and $L_n=E_L/3$. From~\eqref{eq:S4Green} and~\eqref{eq:logPoleComparison},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:S4PoleLogComparison}
 H(n,S^4)=R_n+L_n,\qquad
 R_n=\frac14\int_{-1}^1|A(t)|\,dt,\qquad
 0<L_n\leq\frac{R_n}{n}.
\end{equation}
The parameters in~\eqref{eq:transferParameters} become $b=(1-\varepsilon)/(n+2+\varepsilon)$. Set $\rho=(1+b)/(1-b)=(n+3)/(n+1+2\varepsilon)$. Under the fractional-linear substitution used above, polynomial division gives
\[
 \int_{-1}^1P_1(t)h_b(t)\,d\mu_4(t)=\rho E_1.
\]
Indeed, modulo a polynomial of degree less than $n$, the transformed numerator satisfies $(1-bs)^n/(1-s)=(1-b)^n/(1-s)$. The omitted polynomial integrates to zero against $s_n$.

The transformed logarithmic integral is positive as well. Apart from a polynomial of degree less than $n$, its kernel after substitution is
\[
 (1-bs)^{n-1}\log\frac{1-bs}{1-s}.
\]
Its $n$th derivative is
\[
 n!\int_b^1\frac{(a-b)^{n-1}}{(1-as)^{n+1}}\,da>0,
 \qquad -1<s<1.
\]
This follows by integrating $s/(1-as)$ in $a$ and differentiating after polynomial division. Interpolation at the zeros of $q_{n,4}$ therefore has remainder sign $s_n$, and the moment conditions give $\int Lh_b\,d\mu_4>0$.

The complete folded kernel from~\eqref{eq:foldedElementaryKernels} is $(P_1+\varepsilon L)/3$, up to a constant. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:S4TransferredPotential}
 m^2f_{m,n}(e)=\rho R_n+\frac{\varepsilon}{3}\int_{-1}^1L(t)h_b(t)\,d\mu_4(t)>\rho R_n.
\end{equation}
For $n\geq2$ and even $m\geq4$, we have $\varepsilon\leq1/16$ and
\[
 \rho-\left(1+\frac1n\right)
 =\frac{n-1-2\varepsilon(n+1)}{n(n+1+2\varepsilon)}>0.
\]
Together with~\eqref{eq:S4PoleLogComparison}, this proves $m^2f_{m,n}(e)>H(n,S^4)$. For $n=1$, use $R_1=1/4$ and $H(1,S^4)=1/6+(\log2)/3<2/5$, whereas $\rho R_1\geq8/17>2/5$. Thus
\[
 m^2H(mn,S^4)>H(n,S^4)
\]
for every positive integer $n$ and every even integer $m\geq4$.

To obtain the quantitative estimate, fix $n$ and let $m$ tend to infinity through even integers in~\eqref{eq:S4TransferredPotential}. The functions $h_b$ stay uniformly bounded as $b\to1/(n+2)$, so the logarithmic term tends to zero. The already established limit~\eqref{eq:BohrLimitsFourSix} and~\eqref{eq:transferLowerBound} yield
\[
 \beta_4\geq n^2\frac{n+3}{n+1}R_n.
\]
Combining this with~\eqref{eq:S4PoleLogComparison} proves~\eqref{eq:S4QuantitativeBohr}. For $n\geq2$ its factor is strictly less than one. For $n=1$ the last displayed bound gives $\beta_4\geq1/2>H(1,S^4)$. Thus every finite rescaled constant is strictly below the limit, and their supremum equals that limit.

We now turn to $S^6$. Its kernel~\eqref{eq:S6Green} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:S6ErrorDecomposition}
 H(n,S^6)=\frac{E_2}{15}+\frac{E_1}{5}+\frac{E_L}{5}.
\end{equation}
In this case $b=5(1-\varepsilon)/(3(n+5)-5(1-\varepsilon))$, and the folded kernel is
\[
 F_{m,6}=\frac{P_2}{15}+\frac{10\varepsilon-1}{45}P_1
 +\frac{\varepsilon^2}{5}L+\text{constant}.
\]
For fixed $n$, let $m$ tend to infinity through even integers and put
\[
 b\longrightarrow\frac5{3n+10},\qquad
 x=\frac{b}{1-b}\longrightarrow\frac5{3n+5},\qquad
 \rho=\frac{1+b}{1-b}=1+2x.
\]
The same polynomial division, now keeping two pole terms, gives
\[
 \int P_1h_b\,d\mu_6=\rho^2E_1,\qquad
 \int P_2h_b\,d\mu_6=\rho E_2+\rho(n+1)xE_1.
\]
For the second identity expand $(1-bs)^{n+1}/(1-s)^2$ at $s=1$; the remainder is a polynomial of degree less than $n$ and disappears against $s_n$. Since $h_b$ remains uniformly bounded for fixed $n$, passage to the limit in~\eqref{eq:foldedGreen} is justified. We obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:S6TransferredLimit}
 \begin{aligned}
 \lim_{\substack{m\to\infty\\ m\ \mathrm{even}}}m^2f_{m,n}(e)
 &=F_n,\\
 F_n&=\frac{\rho E_2}{15}
 +\left(\frac{\rho(n+1)x}{15}-\frac{\rho^2}{45}\right)E_1,
 \qquad x=\frac5{3n+5}.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
We shall show that $F_n>H(n,S^6)$ for every $n$.

Let $\lambda=A'(1)$. Root factorization gives $\lambda\geq n$. The simple- and double-pole interpolation remainders used in~\eqref{eq:S6PoleContribution} give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 E_1&=\frac{15}{16}\int_{-1}^1|A(t)|(1-t^2)\,dt,\\
 E_2&=\frac{15}{16}\int_{-1}^1|A(t)|
 \bigl(1+t^2+\lambda(1-t^2)\bigr)\,dt.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Consequently $E_2/E_1\geq n+1$, while~\eqref{eq:logPoleComparison} gives $E_L/E_1\leq1/n$. Since $\rho>1$, these inequalities have the required direction in the difference between~\eqref{eq:S6TransferredLimit} and~\eqref{eq:S6ErrorDecomposition}. For $n\geq3$ they yield
\[
 \frac{45(F_n-H(n,S^6))}{E_1}
 \geq\frac{45n^3+69n^2-345n-225}{n(3n+5)^2}>0.
\]
The numerator, with $k=n-3$, is $45k^3+474k^2+1284k+576$, proving its positivity throughout this range.

The first two degrees require slightly better pole comparisons. For $n=1$, $A(t)=t$ and the displayed integral formulas give $E_2/E_1=4$. Using this value and $E_L/E_1\leq1$ gives $45(F_1-H(1,S^6))/E_1\geq3/8>0$.

For $n=2$, write $A(t)=(t^2-r^2)/(1-r^2)$. The sign moment gives $\int_0^r(1-t^2)^2\,dt=4/15$. At $r=1/3$ the integral is $376/1215>4/15$, so $r<1/3$. Put
\[
 u=\frac{\int_{-1}^1t^2|A(t)|\,dt}{\int_{-1}^1|A(t)|\,dt}.
\]
Bounding the numerator below by its signed integral and the denominator above by the integral of $(t^2+r^2)/(1-r^2)$ gives
\[
 u\geq\frac{1/5-r^2/3}{1/3+r^2}\geq\frac{11}{30}>\frac13.
\]
Thus $E_2/E_1=\lambda+(1+u)/(1-u)\geq4$. Together with $E_L/E_1\leq1/2$, this gives $45(F_2-H(2,S^6))/E_1\geq381/242>0$. The strict comparison is proved for every $n$.

Finally,~\eqref{eq:transferLowerBound},~\eqref{eq:S6TransferredLimit}, and the limit already established in~\eqref{eq:BohrLimitsFourSix} imply
\[
 \beta_6\geq n^2F_n>n^2H(n,S^6)
\]
for every fixed $n$. Taking the supremum and using convergence to $\beta_6$ proves~\eqref{eq:evenBohrSupremum} for $d=6$, completing the proof.
head: environment

label: thm:optimalLinearS2
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first show that an arbitrary linear method cannot have a smaller error. Let $M$ be the supremum in~\eqref{eq:optimalLinearS2} for a fixed operator $A$. We may assume that $M$ is finite. Then $A$ reproduces constants, since all their scalar multiples belong to the class. By scaling, $\left\|f-Af\right\|_\infty\leq M\left\|\Delta f\right\|_\infty$ for every smooth $f$. In particular, $\left\|Af\right\|_\infty\leq\left\|f\right\|_\infty+M\left\|\Delta f\right\|_\infty$, so $A$ is continuous for the $C^2$ topology and the following average is well defined.

For a rotation $Q\in SO(3)$, write $U_Qf(x)=f(Q^{-1}x)$, and average the conjugate operators with respect to normalized Haar measure:
\[
 \widetilde A f=\int_{SO(3)}U_Q^{-1}AU_Qf\,dQ.
\]
Rotations preserve the class, the uniform norm, and $\mathcal H_{<n}$. Each conjugate therefore has the same maximal error $M$, and the triangle inequality gives $\left\|f-\widetilde Af\right\|_\infty\leq M$ throughout the class. Thus averaging does not increase the maximal error.

The averaged operator commutes with rotations. Differentiating along the three one-parameter groups of coordinate rotations shows that it also commutes with $\Delta$, the sum of the squares of their infinitesimal generators. If $Y\in\mathcal H_\ell$ with $\ell\geq n$, then $\widetilde AY$ must have the same Laplacian eigenvalue $-\ell(\ell+1)$ as $Y$. But $\widetilde AY$ belongs to $\mathcal H_{<n}$, where that eigenvalue does not occur, so $\widetilde AY=0$. The spherical harmonic expansion of a smooth function converges in $C^2$; continuity therefore gives $\widetilde Af=0$ whenever $f\perp\mathcal H_{<n}$. On this subclass the approximation error is exactly $\left\|f\right\|_\infty$. Taking its supremum gives $M\geq H(n,S^2)$ by definition~\eqref{eq:sphericalBohrFavard}.

To attain this bound, let $p_{n-1}$ be the best $L^1(dt/2)$ approximant to $G_2$ constructed in Section~\ref{sec:zonalapproximation}, and set
\[
 A_*f(x)=\bar f+\int_{S^2}p_{n-1}(x\cdot y)(-\Delta f)(y)\,d\sigma_2(y),
 \qquad \bar f=\int_{S^2}f\,d\sigma_2.
\]
This is a linear operator with values in $\mathcal H_{<n}$, and it reproduces constants. Applying~\eqref{eq:kernelApproximationBound} to $f-\bar f$ gives $\left\|f-A_*f\right\|_\infty\leq H(n,S^2)$ throughout the class. Together with the lower bound just proved, this establishes~\eqref{eq:optimalLinearS2}.
head: environment

label: thm:strictFavardS2
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We use measures annihilating the approximating polynomials. Equality in the kernel estimate would require the errors with different poles to agree in phase; the annihilation conditions will make this impossible. Compactness then turns the exclusion of equality into a strict bound for the whole class.

Fix $n$, let $p_{n-1}$ be the interpolating polynomial for $G_2$, and put $R_n=G_2-p_{n-1}$. The kernel computations above and rotational invariance give $\int_{S^2}|R_n(x\cdot y)|\,d\sigma_2(y)=H(n,S^2)$ for every pole $x$. Moreover, $\operatorname{sgn} R_n(t)=\operatorname{sgn} U_n(t)$ almost everywhere, so the sign changes precisely at $t_j=\cos(j\pi/(n+1))$, for $j=1,\ldots,n$.

Let $\mathcal M_n$ be the set of finite complex Borel measures on $S^2$ with total variation at most one which annihilate $\mathcal H_{<n}$. For such a measure define
\[
 U_\mu(y)=\int_{S^2}R_n(x\cdot y)\,d\mu(x).
\]
Annihilation of the polynomial part means that this is also the Green potential of $\mu$. The Green representation and Fubini's theorem give $\int f\,d\mu=\int(-\Delta f)U_\mu\,d\sigma_2$ for every smooth $f$. The dual formula for best approximation, followed by the triangle inequality for the potential, therefore yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:S2dualResidualBound}
 K(n,S^2)\leq\sup_{\mu\in\mathcal M_n}\left\|U_\mu\right\|_1\leq H(n,S^2).
\end{equation}
We shall prove that the second inequality is strict.

First, the supremum over measures is attained. The set $\mathcal M_n$ is weak-* compact. Approximate $G_2$ in $L^1(dt/2)$ by continuous functions. For measures of total variation at most one, the error in the corresponding potentials is bounded in $L^1(S^2)$ by the same kernel error, uniformly in the measure. For a continuous kernel, weak-* convergence of a sequence of measures gives pointwise convergence of their potentials, and their uniform boundedness gives convergence in $L^1$. Approximation of $G_2$ thus shows that $\mu\mapsto U_\mu$ is weak-* to $L^1$ continuous on the measure unit ball. It follows that $\left\|U_\mu\right\|_1$ attains its maximum on $\mathcal M_n$.

Suppose that the maximum equals $H(n,S^2)$. The maximizing measure then has total variation one. Write $d\mu=a\,d\nu$, where $\nu=|\mu|$ and $|a|=1$ almost everywhere with respect to $\nu$. Equality in the integrated triangle inequality forces all the contributions to have a common phase for almost every $y$. Thus there is a measurable function $b$, with $|b|=1$ almost everywhere, such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:S2phaseAgreement}
 a(x)\,\operatorname{sgn} R_n(x\cdot y)=b(y)
\end{equation}
for almost every pair $(x,y)$ with respect to $\nu\otimes\sigma_2$. The residual is nonzero almost everywhere for each pole. By Fubini's theorem we may therefore fix a pole $e$ for which this identity holds for almost every $y$. For $\nu$-almost every other pole $x$, the two real sign functions $\operatorname{sgn} R_n(x\cdot y)$ and $\operatorname{sgn} R_n(e\cdot y)$ must agree or be opposite almost everywhere.

This is possible only when $x=e$ or $x=-e$. Indeed, the sign-change curves for a pole $x$ are the circles $x\cdot y=t_j$. If $x$ and $e$ are not parallel, each such circle meets each circle $e\cdot y=t_k$ in at most two points. We can therefore choose a point on a sign-change circle for $x$ which lies on none of those for $e$. In a small neighborhood of that point the sign associated with $e$ is constant, whereas the sign associated with $x$ changes across the circle. Both sides have positive surface measure, contradicting agreement, or opposite agreement, almost everywhere.

Consequently $\mu=A\delta_e+B\delta_{-e}$ for some complex numbers $A$ and $B$. Since $n\geq2$, the measure annihilates both the constant function and the linear function $x\mapsto e\cdot x$. These two conditions give $A+B=0$ and $A-B=0$, hence $\mu=0$. This contradicts its total variation being one. The maximum in~\eqref{eq:S2dualResidualBound} is therefore strictly smaller than $H(n,S^2)$, proving~\eqref{eq:strictFavardS2}.
